doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

title: Music as community and spirit, learning by ear, the money problem
summary: Turré argues music is a cultural, communal expression and objects to the way America has made it about money.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you pass that on to your students? Or try to?

If I think it’s going to make a difference. You know I’ve found that sometimes if you give a student that’s not ready too much you can blow their head and they miss the whole point and get off track in terms of what music is really about. If you look at history, Monk, and look at reality, we live on a musical planet. We’re not the only beings on this planet that make music. Birds sing. Frogs sing. Insects make rhythms and they sing. Dolphins and whales sing. All over there’s musical sounds being made by other creatures. And before written music, before we had MTV and music was about making money, getting over and being famous and wearing something to make people look rather than listen, music was a cultural thing in all the different cultures they had their own music as a means of communication and it’s a collective thing. You have the musicians that make the music, then you have people that listen but they participate. There’s no difference between music and dance and singing. It’s all connected. It’s all an expression of community and consciousness. And that still prevails in traditional African music. America has become about the money. You know to me, you know, I know it’s a reality and you deal with it ‘cause you’ve got to pay your bills, but to me I find it kind of offensive actually, because that’s not what music’s about for me.
So music for you, does it have a spiritual connection of a sort? © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

More than of a sort, it goes back to the essence of life. It’s a reflection of that. Whatever the life condition is it comes out in your music. You can’t fake that. You know we’ve all heard young students say — they’ve got a saxophone and they’ve got great fingers and they can run all the scales. I haven’t really heard any of them could play “Giant Steps” through the keys. But there’s probably a few. But they’re not playing any music. It sounds like they’re playing the computer or something. It sounds like a computer playing back of when you put a score in there and it plays it back for you, it’s something, it’s just mechanical. I don’t feel the spirit. But when you learn to play music as a sound it touches you in a different way. I know if I learn a song by ear I retain it much better than if I read it, if I learn a song by reading. Reading definitely has a place, like for instance, you can’t have a big band ‘cause there’s not enough time to teach everybody their part by rote. You know that’s some time. But I know I played with Dizzy and he would show me some tunes just at the sound check or in the dressing room, and you’ve got to be able to pick them up quick, you know, but he learned it as a sound not from here but from here. The music came into your consciousness through your ears, not through your eyes. The music, when we listen to music it comes through our ears, so to me it’s a big difference there. So I know when I teach I always try to teach somebody something by rote and see how quick they can pick it up, and then they struggle with it, then I’ll give them the music.
